title: An OpenAI model has disproved a central conjecture in discrete geometry | OpenAI
body:
Fields medalist Tim Gowers, writing in the companion paper, calls the result “a milestone in AI mathematics.” According to leading number theorist Arul Shankar, “In my opinion this paper demonstrates that current AI models go beyond just helpers to human mathematicians – they are capable of having original ingenious ideas, and then carrying them out to fruition”.

Mathematicians on the result

1 of 4 [...] This result marks an important moment in the interaction between AI and mathematics: an AI system has autonomously resolved a longstanding open problem at the center of an active field. It also offers an early glimpse of a new kind of collaboration between AI and human mathematicians. In this case, the companion work by external mathematicians paints a substantially richer picture than the original solution alone.

As Thomas Bloom writes in the companion note: [...] Noga Alon

> “There is no doubt that the solution to the unit-distance problem is a milestone in AI mathematics: if a human had written the paper and submitted it to the Annals of Mathematics and I had been asked for a quick opinion, I would have recommended acceptance without any hesitation. No previous AI-generated proof has come close to that.”

title: TurboQuant: Redefining AI efficiency with extreme compression
body:
TurboQuant demonstrates a transformative shift in high-dimensional search. By setting a new benchmark for achievable speed, it delivers near-optimal distortion rates in a data-oblivious manner. This allows our nearest neighbor engines to operate with the efficiency of a 3-bit system while maintaining the precision of much heavier models. See the paper for more details.

## Looking ahead [...] Today, we introduce TurboQuant (to be presented at ICLR 2026), a compression algorithm that optimally addresses the challenge of memory overhead in vector quantization. We also present Quantized Johnson-Lindenstrauss (QJL), and PolarQuant (to be presented at AISTATS 2026), which TurboQuant uses to achieve its results. In testing, all three techniques showed great promise for reducing key-value bottlenecks without sacrificing AI model performance. This has potentially profound implications for [...] Google Research

title: Inside an AI Attack Against a US Retailer
body:
Threat actors have utilized large language models (LLMs) in their attacks as long as the technology has been widely available. Early applications involved generating convincing phishing lures or conducting basic data reconnaissance, but recent evidence shows attackers deploying AI to execute end-to-end attacks, assist with malware development, and more. More recently, attackers have abused — and continue to abuse — agentic penetration testing tools to break into target environments at machine [...] Dick O'Brien, principal intelligence analyst on the Symantec Threat Hunter Team, tells Dark Reading this incident is one of several the team has seen in recent weeks where AI revived an attack. While he calls this a game-changer for attackers, "defenders can potentially leverage that pattern" as AI behaves in a particular kind of way, such as testing variants of a technique in quick succession. [...] Although no vulnerability was exploited and no patching was required, O'Brien believes this trend of AI accelerating attacks is and will continue to affect the patching race. "Our view is that defenders need to start looking at mean time to mitigate rather than mean time to patch. Patching is still important, but it can’t be the only countermeasure."

title: New 'BluePhishing' scam sees criminals spoof AI agents to get access to corporate environments | TechRadar
body:
In a new report, security researchers Proofpoint laid out how a threat actor could create a malicious blueprint in their own Microsoft environment and then - using classic social engineering techniques - convince a victim to approve it in their own environment. To make matters worse, when a malicious agent enters the environment, they can “clone” themselves, creating multiple additional identities, all tasked with doing different things.

Latest Videos FromTechRadar

Watch full video here: [...] Then, they create a link that leads to a genuine Microsoft authorization page. Unlike your run-of-the-mill phishing attack, this one is different because the login page doesn’t need to be fake and spoofed. The attacker does, however, need to have some basic information about the target organization, such as their tenant ID and details about an existing user they can specifically target. [...] One of the first things the AI agent receives, once installed, is a permission called AgentIdentity.CreateAsManager. This allows the threat actor to create additional identities linked to the blueprint that’s now inside their target’s environment. A single blueprint can support up to 250 agent identities, which means there can be a swarm of malicious bots running around at the same time.

title: AI agents are making security’s breakout-time metric obsolete, and no one agrees on what replaces it | VentureBeat
body:
Human attackers at keyboards issue dozens of commands an hour, and AI agents issue about 1,500 an hour, according to Adam Meyers, CrowdStrike’s senior vice president of counter adversary operations.“It’s just speed and volume,” Meyers told VentureBeat. “This is not using new and unseen exploits. It’s just using things that we already knew about, but it’s doing it faster, and it’s kind of connecting the dots at a volume that we’re not used to seeing.” [...] CrowdStrike’s October 21 report profiles four previously unreported attackers the company traced between May and August, and it names Claude Code in all four. CrowdStrike wrote that the four cases “likely demonstrate that agentic AI commoditizes baseline offensive cyber operations.” It saw agents at work because each attacker “left their offensive agent frameworks exposed via open directories,” it wrote. In the Argentine campaign, a “Supervisor” Claude Code agent picked the next task and an [...] The report also says CrowdStrike's threat hunters had already recorded three times as many agentic intrusions in the second half of 2026 as in the first half.

The speed of these attacksis why CrowdStrike is moving away from “breakout time” — the time an intruder needs to move from the first host it compromises to another one on the network — a metric it introduced in 2018 and that the industry has cited ever since. Even CrowdStrike’s own executives have yet to agree on what should replace it.

title: Google broadens its AI hardware portfolio with two new specialized chips | TechCrunch
body: Google is notching up its chipmaking game as the company seeks to reduce its dependence on chips made by other companies for its cloud computing business. Google on Monday unveiled two new variants of its tensor processing units (TPUs), in-house developed chips meant for AI workloads, that broaden its chip portfolio to additional use cases: confidential inference and more memory capacity for large workloads. [...] The new units, TPU 8tx and TPU 8i Max, are part of the company’s eighth generation of chips introduced in April this year, and build on what those chips offered, which was more inference capacity and support for large training requirements. [...] Meanwhile, TPU 8i Max basically combines two of the inference-focused TPU 8i chips the company launched in April, doubling the memory capacity, processing power and bandwidth, but in a single package. The result is a chip that lets AI models handle a larger range of information during queries.

title: Google adds two new specialized chips for AI agents and security to 8th-gen TPU lineup — TPU 8i Max puts two chips on one package for long-context work, TPU 8tx swaps Arm hosts for AMD EPYC | Tom's Hardware
body:
Doubling both SRAM and HBM bandwidth helps keep things scaling, which would put the 8i Max at about 20.2 FP4 PFLOPS, 768 MB SRAM, and about 17.2 TB/s HBM bandwidth. This compares to Nvidia’s Rubin R200 GPU at a rated 50 FP4 PFLOPS for inference and 22 TB/s of HBM4 per socket, or AMD’s MI455X with 40 FP4 PFLOPS. The compute gap is closing. [...] Google's eighth-generation TPU family has now expanded further. Back in April, the company announced TPU 8t for training AI models and TPU 8i for general-purpose inference workloads. Google has now introduced TPU 8tx, built on the same silicon as the previously announced 8t, for confidential, hardware-isolated inference aimed at regulated enterprises and governments, and TPU 8i Max, which combines two 8i chips on one package for long-context agentic work. [...] Coming soon

For the new parts, the TPU 8i Max isn't innovative on the surface, as it’s just two TPU 8i chips combined into a single package. The result is twice the theoretical compute, but more importantly, it fits twice the silicon within the “existing rack footprint,” and Google claims more compute per square foot and per watt.

title: Freedom on the Net 2021: The Global Drive to Control Big Tech | Freedom House
body: The European Union (EU) framework for internet regulation may offer a “third way” between China’s digital authoritarianism and the traditional US emphasis on unrestricted speech and free markets. Two pieces of EU legislation introduced this year—the Digital Services Act (DSA) and the Digital Markets Act—promise to set some positive rules for the tech sector, although democratic policymakers should remain wary of the negative repercussions that their laws could have on internet freedom in more [...] There is still time for democratic governments to pursue smart, narrowly tailored measures to protect users’ rights online. Democracies should push for greater transparency and accountability regarding platforms’ content moderation practices. Data privacy laws should focus on protecting users while preventing greater fragmentation of the internet. And competition policy should foster innovation that responds to user demand for greater personalization, security, and interoperability. Regulation [...] The drive toward national regulation has emerged partly due to a failure to address online harms through self-regulation. The United States played a leading role in shaping early internet norms around free speech and free markets, but its laissez-faire approach to the tech industry created opportunities for authoritarian manipulation, data exploitation, and widespread malfeasance. title: Global Digital Policy Roundup: April 2026 | TechPolicy.Press
body: China’s State Administration for Market Regulation issued a notice on the governance of the internet advertising ecosystem. It requires platforms to regulate advertising ranking systems and bans certain categories of advertising content, including the use of AI to impersonate individuals and content affecting minors. It also issued a notice on enforcement priorities for rectifying the internet advertising market order. title: Global Digital Policy Roundup: August 2026 | TechPolicy.Press
body: China's Cyberspace Administration closed consultation on the Anti-Cyber Violence Law, covering content moderation regulation, content moderation authority governance, and user rights, which would require platforms to establish monitoring and rumor-refutation mechanisms for cyberbullying.
